references.text: Jesus teaches the disciples that whoever wants to be great among them must be their servant, and that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Direct parallel to the theme of service and greatness in Matt 20:25-28.
Mark's parallel where Jesus says that the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42-45).
Jesus concretely demonstrates his role as servant by washing the disciples' feet – a practical fulfillment of the words "I am among you as one who serves" (John 13:4-5).
After the foot washing, Jesus explains that as their Lord and Teacher he has given them an example: they should serve one another just as he has served them (John 13:12-17).
Jesus says that whoever is greatest among you must be your servant, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled – the same theme of greatness through service (Matt 23:11-12).
Earlier in Luke, Jesus teaches that whoever is least among all of you, he is great – a parallel to the question of who is greatest (Luke 9:48).
Paul describes Christ as one who took the form of a servant and humbled himself – a theological elaboration of Jesus' words that he is among them as the one who serves (Phil 2:5-8).
Jesus promises blessing to those servants who are awake, and says that the master himself will tie his apron and serve them – an image of the Lord serving (Luke 12:37).

The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven, and Jesus answers that whoever makes himself small like a child is the greatest – the same fundamental question about greatness (Matt 18:1-4).
Paul points to Christ's example: Christ did not live to please himself but served others – a reflection of Jesus' self-understanding as servant (Rom 15:3).
